q: The Doppler effect or Doppler shift is the change in frequency of a wave related to an observer due to the relative motion between the source and observer.
e: This is the precise definition of the Doppler effect.

q: It is named after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler, who described the phenomenon in 1842.
e: This provides the historical origin of the effect's name.

q: Usually, only the motion of the source and the observer directly towards or away from each other in the reference frame in which the wave medium is considered at rest.
e: This is the standard simplification used when introducing the Doppler equation.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of frequency (pitch) heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: This is the classic real-world example used to explain the Doppler effect.

q: A common example of Doppler shift is the change of amplitude heard when a vehicle sounding a horn approach and recedes from an observer.
e: The Doppler shift is a change in frequency (pitch), not amplitude.

q: There are three cases we encounter in Doppler effect.
e: The textbook categorizes the Doppler effect into three specific cases of relative motion.

q: $f_o$ is frequency heard by the observer.
e: This defines the variable $f_o$ in the Doppler equation.

q: $f_s$ is frequency produced by the source.
e: This defines the variable $f_s$ in the Doppler equation.

q: $v$ is speed of sound in the medium.
e: This defines the variable $v$ in the Doppler equation.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves towards the source.
e: Moving towards the source increases the observed frequency, requiring a positive numerator.

q: $+v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: When moving away, $-v_o$ is used to decrease the observed frequency.

q: $-v_o$ is used when the observer moves away from the source.
e: Moving away decreases the observed frequency.

q: $-v_s$ is used when the source moves towards the observer.
e: A source moving towards the observer compresses wavelengths, requiring a smaller denominator.

q: $+v_s$ is used when the source moves away from the observer.
e: A source moving away stretches wavelengths, requiring a larger denominator.

q: When observer and source are stationary, $v_o = v_s = 0$.
e: If there is no relative motion, the velocity terms in the equation become zero.

q: The wavelength of light from a star observed from the earth shifts towards the red end of the spectrum when the earth and the star are moving away from each other.
e: This describes the astronomical red shift caused by the Doppler effect.

q: This phenomenon is called red shift.
e: Red shift is the specific term for light stretching to longer wavelengths.

q: The phenomenon of light shifting towards the red end of the spectrum is called blue shift.
e: Shifting to the red end is red shift; blue shift occurs when objects approach.

q: The velocity of the astronomical body moving away from the earth can be determined from the fractional change in wavelength.
e: Astronomers use this fractional change to calculate the recession velocity of stars.

q: If the star were approaching the earth the spectral lines would shift towards blue end.
e: Approach compresses light waves, shifting them to shorter (blue) wavelengths.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses electromagnetic waves instead of sound.
e: Radar applies the echo principle using radio waves rather than acoustic waves.

q: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses sound waves instead of electromagnetic waves.
e: Radar uses electromagnetic waves, whereas sonar uses sound waves.

q: The Doppler effect is used in some types of radar, to measure the velocity of detected objects.
e: Doppler radar is specifically designed to calculate object speed.

q: Doppler ultrasound is a technique that is used to examine blood flow.
e: This is a primary medical application of the Doppler effect.

q: Blood flow rates can be found by measuring Doppler shift in frequency of ultrasound reflected by red blood cell (known as angiodynography).
e: Red blood cells act as moving reflectors, allowing flow rate calculation.

q: This technique can help reveal blockage to blood flow, show the formation of plaque in arteries and provide detailed information on the heartbeat of the fetus during labor and delivery.
e: These are key diagnostic capabilities of Doppler ultrasound in medicine.

q: It can also be used to examine organ such as heart (echocardiography) and kidney.
e: Echocardiography is a specific type of Doppler ultrasound used for the heart.
